prompt:
A 28-year-old woman with asthma reports daytime symptoms most days, nighttime awakenings twice weekly, and rescue inhaler use several times per week despite good adherence to low-dose inhaled corticosteroid. Inhaler technique is verified as adequate and she has no ongoing tobacco exposure. What is the appropriate approach to her uncontrolled asthma?

Provide a stepwise therapeutic management plan including medications, counseling, and follow-up.

rubric_items.text: Step up controller therapy by adding a long-acting beta-agonist to the inhaled corticosteroid or by increasing to medium-dose inhaled corticosteroid therapy.
Use inhaled corticosteroid-formoterol as maintenance-and-reliever therapy when available and appropriate for the prescribed regimen.
Reinforce continued controller adherence and correct inhaler technique during ongoing asthma care.
Identify and address asthma triggers and relevant comorbidities such as allergic rhinitis, gastroesophageal reflux, and obesity.
Provide a written asthma action plan.
Arrange follow-up after treatment escalation to reassess symptom control, reliever use, and adverse effects.
Refer for specialist assessment of biologic eligibility if asthma remains severe or refractory after optimized standard therapy.
Obtain spirometry to confirm variable airflow limitation and assess lung function.
Assess exacerbation risk, including prior emergency visits, hospitalizations, and systemic corticosteroid courses.
Ensure continued access to an appropriate reliever inhaler after controller therapy is stepped up.
Prescribe a long-acting beta-agonist as monotherapy without an inhaled corticosteroid.
Prescribe chronic daily oral corticosteroids before optimizing inhaled controller therapy.
Rely solely on increased short-acting beta-agonist use to control her symptoms.
Discontinue inhaled corticosteroid therapy.
Continue the unchanged low-dose inhaled corticosteroid regimen despite persistent uncontrolled symptoms.
Start a biologic agent now without first optimizing standard inhaled therapy and establishing biologic eligibility.
Give a routine burst of systemic corticosteroids in the absence of an acute exacerbation.
Prescribe empiric antibiotics for chronic asthma symptoms without evidence of bacterial infection.
Replace inhaled corticosteroid therapy with leukotriene-receptor-antagonist monotherapy as the primary step-up strategy.
Escalate directly from low-dose to high-dose inhaled corticosteroid without first using a standard intermediate step-up option.
Add a long-acting muscarinic antagonist before trying an inhaled corticosteroid-long-acting beta-agonist regimen.
Start theophylline instead of an inhaled corticosteroid-based step-up regimen.
